title: Triage Software for Satellite-SOS Rescue Teams
one_liner: Intake, deduplication and dispatch software for county and volunteer search-and-rescue teams flooded by satellite SOS messages.
customer: County sheriff SAR coordinators, state SAR coordinators, national park services and mountain rescue organizations.
problem: As satellite texting reaches ordinary phones, more people go remote and press SOS. Rescuers receive short, delayed, asynchronous messages with weak location data and many false alarms. Coordination centers were built for 911 voice calls, and volunteer teams run on spreadsheets and group texts.
solution: A gateway that ingests SOS relays (email, API, text) from phone makers and satellite messaging providers, deduplicates, geolocates, and adds terrain and weather context. It runs structured 160-character question flows, recommends the resource type to dispatch, and keeps a log for after-action review and cost recovery.
why_now: Satellite messaging on unmodified phones went mainstream across 2025-26 (the briefing shows new carrier launches as late as Sept 28, 2026). AST and SpaceX D2C are scaling, and phone makers are adding satellite SOS. The receiving end has not been rebuilt.
revenue_model: $3-15k per year per county or team. State-level contracts of $50-200k. Optional paid membership or SAR-insurance partnership.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck moved from sending distress to receiving and triaging it. Whoever owns the receive-side workflow becomes the system of record, and public agencies pay for it out of existing rescue budgets.
first_30_days: Shadow three volunteer SAR teams and one state coordinator. Build a minimal intake and dedupe tool that runs alongside their current tools. Offer it free for one summer season in exchange for a paid annual contract.

title: Executive Physicals for Union Trades Members
one_liner: Mobile 'Physical Days' at union halls and apprenticeship centers that give tradespeople the CEO-style cardiometabolic checkup, sold to the multiemployer health funds that pay their claims.
customer: Trustees and administrators of Taft-Hartley multiemployer health and welfare funds (building trades, Teamsters, food and commercial workers) and self-insured municipal and transit plans. First buyer: the fund of a 2,000-member electricians' or pipefitters' local.
problem: Workers 45-64 in the trades carry high rates of hypertension, sleep apnea, hearing loss, silica or dust lung exposure and undetected heart disease, yet they work 6am shifts and cannot make weekday clinic hours. Funds face rising costs (employers say GLP-1 drug costs loom large in the 2026 Business Group on Health survey) but their prevention is a voucher for an annual physical with low uptake. Corporate wellness vendors are built for white-collar campuses, not job sites.
solution: A 45-minute station circuit at the union hall or training center: validated blood pressure, fingerstick lipids and A1c (ApoB by send-out), single-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation, spirometry for dusty trades, audiogram, a STOP-BANG screen with a hand-off home sleep test, grip and gait, and FIT kits. A physician or NP reviews results the same day. Intermediate-risk members get a pre-booked $75-150 coronary calcium scan at a partner imaging center, and members with findings get a fast lane through a care navigator. Occupation-specific add-ons: sleep apnea for drivers, hearing and silica for construction. Fixed-fee pricing with no referral kickbacks.
why_now: GLP-1 spending has made plan sponsors receptive to prevention offsets. Point-of-care devices are now small and cheap enough to run a full circuit from two suitcases. Skilled-trades labor is aging and scarce, so trustees have a genuine interest in keeping members working and healthy longer.
revenue_model: $150-250 per participant paid by the fund, quarterly repeat days, plus optional shared-savings on downstream claims after the first year; add-on family-member days for spouses.
non_obvious_insight: Unions and multiemployer funds are the last pooled buyer with a 30-year time horizon on each member, so they are among the few payers who can actually capture the return on prevention (a corporate employer loses the employee after three years). Trustees are elected by the workers, so 'the same physical executives pay $5,000 for' is politically powerful. Elite prevention has to be sold where the payer keeps the member long enough to profit.
first_30_days: Get an introduction through an apprenticeship training center director or a local business manager. Offer a free or at-cost Physical Day for 40 members, staffed by a physician partner and two techs (roughly $6k in costs). Collect anonymized data on undiagnosed hypertension, high ApoB, apnea risk and hearing loss. Bring a one-page summary to the trustees at their next quarterly meeting comparing the cost of 30 physicals to one avoided cardiac event. Aim to sign a recurring contract within 4-5 months.

title: Teleoperated Trenching Crews for Infill Lots
one_liner: A control room of remote operators driving retrofitted compact excavators and skid steers on residential lots (utility trenching, pad grading, backfill), sold per linear foot.
customer: Small and ADU builders, factory-built home dealers needing site work, and small site-work contractors short on operators.
problem: Site work and foundations are the first constraint (foundations wait 30+ days; 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks). Operators are aging out and are poached by larger jobs. Small residential jobs waste an operator's day on travel and waiting.
solution: Rental compact excavators fitted with joystick actuation, cameras, cellular or satellite bonding and a geofence kill-switch. Operators, including 55+ or injured veterans, run machines from a control room, one job after another across a metro, while a local machine tender handles spotting and moves. Start with the lowest-risk tasks in fenced residential lots and sell by linear foot.
why_now: Teleoperation retrofit kits and satellite or 5G links are now off-the-shelf. Autonomous pile drivers already work commercially on solar sites, proving field-robot acceptance. Enforcement and the labor squeeze are thinning site crews.
revenue_model: $175-225 per operated machine-hour or per-linear-foot pricing. Retrofit and rental margin. Later, software licensing to sitework contractors.
non_obvious_insight: The unlock is not autonomy, which is hard, but operator pooling. A person on site wastes half a day traveling and idling, whereas a remote operator can serve many small jobs, and older or injured operators can keep working. Small lots become profitable.
first_30_days: Rent one compact excavator and buy a retrofit or factory remote kit. Test in a closed lot with a safety case and insurance broker input. Sign 3 ADU or factory-home dealers for trenching on fenced lots. Run the first paid jobs with a spotter present.

title: Hotel Strike Early-Warning for Event Planners
one_liner: A subscription database and parametric cover that tells meeting and group planners which contracted hotels' labour contracts expire before their event, and pays out if a strike hits.
customer: Association and corporate meeting planners, incentive houses, sports and event organisers and tour operators that contract 100+ room-night blocks 12-24 months ahead.
problem: Chicago hotel workers authorised a strike at 85%, potentially the largest in the city's history, and a Seattle Hilton strike lasted 85 days. Planners contract blocks years ahead and learn about labour risk from the news. Strike coverage under contract clauses is vague, and relocating an event on short notice costs heavily.
solution: Track union contract expirations, strike votes and bargaining status per property, from union pages, filings and news. Score each hotel and date for strike risk, alert planners, and provide a labour-disruption clause template. Later add parametric cover underwritten by an MGA that pays per room-night if a strike affects a contracted property.
why_now: Hotel labour unrest is elevated in 2026, hotel costs have repriced sharply, and hotel operators are cutting staff citing AI (Mews cut 15%). Planners are more exposed to relocation than ever.
revenue_model: USD 3-8K per year per planning team, cover premiums of about 1.5-3% of block value, and broker fees.
non_obvious_insight: A strike is a scheduled event, not a surprise. Contract expiry dates are public, yet the buyers of long-dated blocks bear the tail risk and nobody prices it.
first_30_days: Compile a spreadsheet of union contract expirations for the top 40 US convention cities from union local sites and news. Publish a free '2027 events at risk' report to planner communities, then convert responders to a USD 2K annual subscription. Line up an MGA for the cover after the first 10 customers.

title: Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores
one_liner: Evidence packs showing a coarse satellite-derived wildfire score is wrong about one specific lot, filed under new statutory appeal rights.
customer: Independent insurance agents and HOAs or fire-safe councils in Colorado and California whose clients face nonrenewal or surcharges. Insurers' appeal desks are a later buyer.
problem: Colorado HB25-1182 (in force since July 1, 2026) makes insurers disclose the parcel's score, credit documented mitigation and offer an appeal. California AB 75, operative July 1, 2026, gives notice and dispute rights over aerial-imagery nonrenewals. But 'owners still have to prove their case', and many wildfire models lean on roughly 30 m fuel layers and stale imagery that misclassify irrigated, gravel-scaped or recently cleared lots.
solution: For each parcel, pull the disclosed model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density, distance to wildland) and overlay multi-date 15-50 cm satellite imagery showing vegetation change, roof material and clearance, plus dated homeowner photos. Produce a regulator-format rebuttal pack with a ranked list of cheap fixes, and give agents a dashboard that scans their whole book for likely score errors. The real edge is a growing database of which input errors insurers concede.
why_now: Both disclosure-and-appeal regimes went live in July 2026 and insurers' appeal desks are unprepared. Commercial constellations, including 30 cm Pelican and Vantor archives, plus 15 cm HD, have made high-resolution archives cheap. Regulators in CT, NH and PA say imagery alone is insufficient, and NY has a pending bill.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per parcel via agents. $10-$25 per parcel per year for HOA book scans. About $60 per appeal from insurers for standardised evidence intake.
non_obvious_insight: Wildfire scores are averages of coarse layers, so the cheapest way to change a score is often to fix an input error rather than harden the house. The resolution gap between 30 m models and 30 cm imagery is systematic, so a win on one lot tends to generalise to its neighbours and compounds into a book-level lever for agents.
first_30_days: Pick the Colorado Front Range. Recruit 5 independent agencies with 200+ WUI clients each, plus 2 HOAs. Run the first 50 score disclosures at a $99 pilot price per file, and track appeal success rate as the marketing asset.

title: Plug-In Electrification Kits for Landlords
one_liner: Sell curated no-new-circuit kits (120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps, induction, balcony solar) to small landlords and housing authorities as an electrician-light retrofit.
customer: Small landlords (1-50 units), property managers and public housing authorities. Utilities and state HEAR programs co-fund the kits.
problem: Data centers pay electricians 25-30% more, so residential contractors cannot staff jobs. Panel upgrades cost $1,500-5,000. Renters and multifamily have no obvious product, and landlords have no reason to pay for tenants' savings.
solution: A packaged program with approved plug-in devices only (UL 3700 balcony solar in states that legalized it, 120V heat pump water heaters, window heat pumps). Maintenance staff or a handyman installs them. The company handles rebate stacking, a lease addendum and tenant paperwork, an insurance rider, and remote monitoring. It also sells a landlord 'plug-in policy in a box' for HOAs and condo boards.
why_now: Nine states had signed plug-in solar laws by September 2026 and UL 3700 now exists. 120V heat pump water heaters and window heat pumps arrived, and housing-authority window heat pump rollouts show large buyers exist. Labor scarcity makes no-electrician products the path of least resistance.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on $1.5-4k kits, a per-unit administration fee from utility and state programs, and SaaS for portfolio managers.
non_obvious_insight: The electrician shortage is the binding constraint, so design products that do not need one. Renter electrification will run through plug-ins, and whoever writes the landlord's compliance and insurance paperwork controls distribution.
first_30_days: Pick two plug-in-friendly states. Assemble a three-SKU kit from existing vendors. Pitch 20 small landlord associations and two housing authorities. Sell 20 kits. Get an insurer's written OK on the rider language.

title: Cash Caregiver Rails: Deductible, Reimbursable, Legal
one_liner: Payroll plus clinician plan-of-care paperwork that turns cash-paid family and neighbor caregivers into tax-deductible, insurance-reimbursable, workers'-comp-covered employment.
customer: Adult children and spouses who pay $15-30 an hour in cash to informal home aides for a parent with dementia, frailty or serious illness. The households spend $20-60K a year, and some have long-term care insurance.
problem: A large slice of elder home care runs on cash, word of mouth and no paperwork. Families lose tax deductions and long-term care insurance benefits that require documentation. They carry unlimited liability for injuries in their home and owe unpaid household-employer taxes. The aide has no wage record, comp cover, or path to benefits. Agencies solve this at $35+ an hour, which many families can't afford.
solution: An employer-of-record service for family-hired caregivers. It provides payroll, tax filing (household employer) and workers' comp or injury cover. A telehealth nurse practitioner certifies chronic illness and writes a plan of care, which are the tax and long-term care insurance requirements for 'qualified long-term care services'. A claims-ready packet is generated for long-term care insurers and the family's tax preparer, and a shift-check-in log is kept. Optional backup-aide pool for absences.
why_now: Boomers are in their 80s. Agency costs keep rising, and 2025-26 Medicaid funding cuts push more families toward informal care. Telehealth nurse practitioner visits make chronic-illness certification cheap. Household payroll rails and workers'-comp programs for single-worker households are now easy to embed through APIs.
revenue_model: $99-149 per household per month platform fee plus payroll processing. An annual $150-250 clinician certification fee. An insurer-paid fee, or employer benefit contract, for claim-ready documentation that reduces fraud and denial disputes. Backup-aide shifts at a margin.
non_obvious_insight: Families don't pay for compliance. They pay when the paperwork unlocks money that is currently being left on the table: deductions and insurance benefits that are only available to a documented, plan-of-care relationship. The clinician certification is the wedge, and payroll is just plumbing. Selling it as 'get reimbursed' rather than 'stay legal' changes conversion completely. It also builds a data asset that insurers will pay for.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax-preparer network or elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers who see cash caregivers daily. Contract a telehealth nurse practitioner group for plan-of-care certifications. Use an existing household payroll provider under white-label. Sign 15 families at $99/month with a money-back guarantee tied to documented reimbursements. Measure recovered dollars per household as the headline metric.

title: Proof-of-Ingestion Traps for Creators' Content
one_liner: Plant unique, statistically detectable traps in creators' work, then probe AI models to produce evidence that the content was ingested.
customer: Newsletter, blog and podcast networks, small publishers, illustrator collectives and rights-holder collectives, plus litigation funders and law firms.
problem: Creators cannot prove that a model trained on their work, and that proof is the gating evidence for licensing and claims. Published research on copyright traps and 'radioactive' data suggests unique planted sequences can statistically reveal training use. The licensing market is forming (Suno's licensed model, label suits, Spotify deals), but information is heavily asymmetric.
solution: A plug-in adds unique fictional-but-plausible facts and phrasing patterns to text posts (and validated perturbations where it works for images and audio). A monitoring service queries major model APIs monthly with probes and issues an 'ingestion report' with p-values. Reports aggregate into collective evidence packs for licensing negotiations and claims. Detection power depends on repetition and model behavior, so start with text.
why_now: AI licensing and settlements are creating demand for evidence, probing APIs are cheap, and trap research has matured enough to productize.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per creator, $2-10k/month for publishers and collectives, $25-100k per litigation-grade study, and a fee share on licensing deals.
non_obvious_insight: Whoever produces credible evidence of ingestion becomes the toll-taker between creators and labs, like a credit bureau for training data. Traps are cheap to plant, while the evidence is priced like litigation support.
first_30_days: Seed traps in three months of posts across 20 newsletters, test six popular models with retrieval off, and publish a results note. Take a sample report to two litigation-funding shops and small-publisher trade groups.

title: Asset-Light Black Mass Desk Under BIS Rule
one_liner: A trading and compliance desk that becomes the default outlet for US black mass sellers, using the rule's toll-processing exception instead of building plants.
customer: Scrap managers at US cell gigafactories and black-mass aggregators (sellers), who pay brokerage and compliance fees. Toll processors with idle hydromet capacity pay for feed access.
problem: Since the Aug 27, 2026 BIS/DPA rule, sellers must allocate 100% of monthly black mass sales to US buyers. Domestic buyers are thin after Ascend's Chapter 11 and Li-Cycle's bankruptcy, and DOE grants were cancelled. Sellers face legal exposure, a one-sided bid, and assay disputes. BIS has said more materials may be added.
solution: A desk that (1) certifies sampling and assay per lot, (2) documents and allocates monthly volumes across US buyers, (3) structures toll-processing corridors. These run through domestic hydromet capacity, or through foreign processors whose intermediates return to the US, which the rule exempts. (4) It issues a per-lot compliance file. It never owns a plant, only feedstock relationships and the legal wrapper.
why_now: The BIS temporary final rule (Aug 2026) makes domestic allocation mandatory and toll-processing the only export route. Manufacturing scrap is about two-thirds of North American battery feedstock through 2030, so the flow is real. Capex-heavy players have just failed.
revenue_model: 2-4% brokerage on lot value, $1-3K per-lot assay and compliance-file fee, toll-margin on structured deals, and a monthly subscription for allocation reporting.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders read Ascend and Li-Cycle as proof that battery recycling does not work. They actually proved that owning capex ahead of feedstock timing does not work. The BIS rule turned feedstock rights plus a legal wrapper into the scarce asset, and the money sits between captive sellers and stranded capacity.
first_30_days: Read the rule with a trade lawyer and publish a 6-page 'what this means for sellers' note. Cold-call scrap managers at cell plants and the top 10 aggregators. Sign 2-3 non-exclusive brokerage LOIs. Collect toll price sheets from 2 US processors and 1 Asian or European processor. Target the first structured lot in about 90 days.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

title: Volumetric Concert Replays for Small Venues
one_liner: A multi-camera Gaussian-splat capture rig that lets attendees of 200-2,000 capacity shows buy a free-viewpoint replay of their favorite songs.
customer: Independent venues, promoters and mid-tier touring acts, with ticket-holders as end buyers at $5-15 per replay.
problem: Small acts earn only from tickets and merch, and concert film needs a crew. Sphere grossed $420.5M in 2024 but is for superstars. Fans want to relive the night from where they stood, and no affordable product delivers it.
solution: A 12-24 camera synced rig hung on lighting truss, cloud splat processing, and a phone and headset web viewer. Attendees unlock replays via a ticket QR code. Start with one or two songs with static cameras and add motion later, with revenue shared with the venue and artist.
why_now: 4D Gaussian splatting hit practical quality and cost in 2025-26, web viewers are mature, and headsets are common enough to matter.
revenue_model: $2-5k capture fee per show or free capture with 50% of replay sales, plus venue subscription for archives.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the film but the fan's own position. Selling 'the replay from where I stood' to the 300 people who attended targets a captive small market with high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Build a 12-camera rig for about $8k. Capture 3 local shows in exchange for rights. Test QR-code replay sales at the merch table and measure conversion.

title: Scam-Spell Breakers: Human Callbacks for Seniors
one_liner: A human 'callback' service in which ex-call-center agents are trained to talk older customers out of scams, sold to credit unions and community banks as a per-member protection benefit.
customer: Community banks and credit unions (5k-200k members), also Medicare Advantage plans, and families via a $19/month consumer plan. Banks pay about $0.40-1.00 per member per month or $75-150 per intervention.
problem: The FBI's 2025 IC3 report (April 2026) shows Americans over 60 lost $7.75B, up 59%, with more than 3,100 senior complaints citing AI. Detection systems flag transactions, but victims coached by scammers ignore warnings and lie to tellers. Frontline staff lack the time and training for the delicate conversation that breaks the scammer's hold without shaming the victim.
solution: When a bank's system flags a large or unusual transfer by a senior, the transaction is held and a trained spell-breaker calls within minutes. They use scam-specific playbooks (romance, crypto investment, tech support) based on motivational interviewing, guide the customer to verify independently with a trusted family member, and document the outcome. They also enroll a trusted-contact circle and run monthly check-ins. Reports show dollars saved per dollar of fees.
why_now: Elder-fraud losses and AI-voice-clone scams are rising sharply, while banks face regulatory and reputational pressure to show duty of care. Call-center layoffs create a large pool of people with exactly this skill set.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month bank contracts, per-intervention fees, a consumer family plan, and outcome-based bonuses tied to verified saves.
non_obvious_insight: Scam interception is a rapport problem, not a detection problem, and the best call-center agents' skills of de-escalation, listening, and warm scripts transfer directly. The ROI is unusually crisp for a services business: dollars saved versus fees, which gives an easy pitch to a CFO or board.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 ex-agents and train them with retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Approach 3 credit unions through state leagues and offer a 90-day, success-priced pilot using the credit union's existing fraud alerts and a purely phone-based workflow. Aim for one paid pilot within 60-90 days.

title: Lot Vault: Reagent Warranty Claims and Lot Registry
one_liner: A photo-the-label app that files unclaimed reagent-guarantee refunds for labs, quietly builds the only lot-level reagent performance database, and then group-buys locked good lots for small labs.
customer: Lab managers and PIs in organoid, iPSC, primary-immune-cell and antibody-heavy labs (about $79-199/month per lab). Core facilities and departments with central purchasing pay for the site-wide tier. Later, challenger reagent vendors and distributors pay for lot-level analytics.
problem: Every experienced postdoc knows the hidden variable behind failed experiments is the reagent lot: FBS, Matrigel/BME, B27, human serum, antibodies, polymerases. A lot that passes the vendor's certificate of analysis can still kill your organoids, and nobody logs lot numbers. Vendors' satisfaction guarantees require the lot number, images and a claim inside a time window, so postdocs almost never file. Money goes unclaimed. Six labs across town hit the same bad lot and never find out. When a good lot runs out, a two-year experimental series has to be re-validated.
solution: Wedge: a phone app where the postdoc snaps the vial label and taps 'worked' or 'failed', with optional gel or blot photos. On 'failed' it drafts the vendor guarantee claim with lot, dates and images, and tracks the credit. On 'worked' it logs the lot against the user's cell type and assay. Over time this becomes a crowd-sourced registry: 'Matrigel lot X: 7 of 9 organoid labs report failure.' Phase 2: when a lot shows good in at least 5 labs, the company negotiates a vendor lot reservation and runs a pooled group buy. Small labs get a locked lot for 12-24 months without needing 100 bottles of freezer space. The company takes a 10-15% margin.
why_now: NIH funding disruption and higher reagent prices from tariffs (verify current tariff levels) make labs care about every wasted dollar in 2025-26. Vision LLMs make label OCR and claim drafting almost free. Reproducibility pressure is high and the NIH is pushing rigor. Vendors are consolidating, and challenger brands need a credible independent signal to displace incumbents.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab or per core. A 10-15% margin on group-buy locked-lot sales. Success-fee or flat fee on recovered credits. Later, paid lot-analytics dashboards for challenger vendors and distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The certificate of analysis tests the vendor's assay, not yours. The only real lot-quality signal is 'the lab down the hall using my cell type', and that signal already circulates informally by hallway lore. Nobody has digitized it because no single lab has enough data. The warranty-claim refund is the Trojan horse: it gives the user immediate ROI, so people log lot numbers without being asked, and it produces the data moat.
first_30_days: Build a no-code MVP: a forwarding inbox plus a form that pulls lot number and catalog number and drafts claim emails. Recruit 15 labs from organoid and iPSC Slack and Discord channels and postdoc association lists. Offer 3 months free plus a 'we file it for you' concierge. File the first 30 claims by hand to learn each vendor's rules. Show each lab the dollars recovered. Convert to $99/month once the first credit lands. In parallel, pick one product (for example BME or FBS) and quote a pooled lot reservation to 10 pilot labs.

title: Tell Us Once: US Death-Event Switchboard
one_liner: Verify an executor once, then let agents notify and close dozens of institutions for you, building toward a reusable 'authority to act' credential the institutions accept.
customer: Executors and surviving families pay, with distribution through funeral homes, estate attorneys and employers or insurers. Institutions later pay per verified case.
problem: US executors call dozens of banks, card issuers, utilities and subscription companies, each demanding its own certified death certificate, letters and forms. The deceased's identity is exposed to fraud. The UK has 'Tell Us Once', the US has nothing, and the brief finds no dominant software owner of the estate close-out workflow.
solution: The executor uploads the death certificate, ID and letters. The system verifies them once, then voice and browser agents run institution-specific playbooks: credit bureau alerts, identity locks, marketing suppression, subscription and utility cancellations or transfers, date-of-death balance requests and claim forms. A status board tracks every account, and human ops handle exceptions. Over time it issues a verified executor credential institutions accept by API.
why_now: Voice agents that navigate phone trees and hold queues, and browser agents that complete web forms, reached usable reliability in 2025-26. Digital ID wallets are spreading. Insurer and employer channels such as Empathy (50M+ covered policyholders) show buyers for bereavement services, but Empathy is not a close-out execution layer.
revenue_model: $199-$399 flat per estate ($99 wholesale to funeral homes), $10-$40 per verified case from institutions, and insurer or employer benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is repeated verification, not the work itself. A reusable, verified authority credential collapses 60 identical fights into one and gives institutions a fraud-reduction reason to cooperate.
first_30_days: Build playbooks for the top 30 institutions (big banks, card issuers, brokers, telecoms, streaming, credit bureaus). Sell 25 human-in-the-loop cases through 5 funeral homes at $149. Record each institution's requirements to build the data moat.

title: Defense Magnet and Tungsten Provenance Dossiers
one_liner: A shared investigator that produces audit-ready provenance files on magnets and tungsten parts for the sub-tier suppliers who cannot get answers from their distributors.
customer: Small and mid-size defense sub-tier suppliers (motors, actuators, sensors, drones, speakers) that buy NdFeB, SmCo magnets or tungsten parts through distributors.
problem: DFARS magnet and tungsten sourcing restrictions extend to upstream mining and refining stages from January 2027. Small suppliers cannot compel Chinese-linked distributors or sinterers to disclose provenance, and primes will demand attestations.
solution: A dossier per part family: supplier questionnaires, document and mill-cert review, distributor-to-sinterer trace-back, and optional lab fingerprinting (trace-element and isotopic) via partner labs. It includes an attestation vault ready for prime audits and an approved-source list of non-covered and recycled suppliers.
why_now: The January 2027 DFARS deadline is about three months away as of late September 2026. Government equity deals (MP, Lithium Americas) and the BIS scrap rule show that provenance is now a national-security control.
revenue_model: $4-15K per part family, $1-3K monthly subscription for upkeep and alerts, and lab-test pass-through with margin.
non_obvious_insight: This is a paperwork problem too small for any customer to solve alone. A shared investigator with a growing fingerprint library amortizes the cost across dozens of clients and gets cheaper as it scales.
first_30_days: Build a free 'does this part need proof?' checker. Pull sub-tier contractors from public procurement records and reach out to 100 firms with the January deadline. Line up a partner lab for fingerprinting. Close 5 paid dossiers.

title: Turn Gray-Market Retatrutide Demand Into Trial Enrollment
one_liner: Intercept people searching to buy unapproved obesity drugs and route them, screened, to active trials that pay by the qualified referral.
customer: CROs, sponsors and trial sites running obesity and metabolic trials (paying per qualified lead or randomized patient), with the consumer as the traffic source.
problem: Sponsors struggle to recruit GLP-1-naive participants because prior GLP-1 use is an exclusion criterion and 22% of households already have a user. Meanwhile, non-trial retatrutide use grew ~1.8x per quarter, 71% of traced users bought outside trials, and Australia issued a liver and kidney injury alert in Jun 2026.
solution: A compliance-reviewed 'legitimate access' site and search and social funnel that meets intent ('retatrutide', 'triple agonist'), explains the risks, pre-screens (BMI, comorbidities, naive or washout status, geography) and refers to nearby enrolling Phase 2/3 sites. It screens out people who already took unapproved product where the protocol excludes them, and sponsors pay on qualified referral or randomization.
why_now: Retatrutide's Phase 3 program and Lilly's planned Q1 2027 filing are peak-hype. FDA and Lilly takedowns (>14,000 listings) push searchers toward risk. Pills at $149 are draining the classic trial pool, so recruitment cost per patient is rising.
revenue_model: Est. $150-500 per qualified referral and $2-6k per randomized patient, paid by CROs and sites, with performance tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Enforcement cannot remove demand. The highest-intent audience in obesity pharmacology is currently monetized by gray-market vendors, while trial sponsors pay per head for exactly the same people.
first_30_days: Build three landing pages and a screener reviewed by a regulatory consultant. Register with 3-5 enrolling sites and one CRO recruiter. Spend ~$3k on search and social ads for 'retatrutide clinical trial' style queries (check ad-policy limits) and deliver the first 50 pre-screened leads on a pay-per-qualified-referral contract.

title: Lend Against Battery Earnings for Vet Bills
one_liner: A wallet that routes VPP and demand-response payouts into a dedicated pet-care fund, then advances emergency vet money against the battery's telemetry-verified future earnings.
customer: Home-battery owners in VPPs (repayment via payout offset). Partners who pay are VPP aggregators and retail energy providers (retention) and pet insurers (customer acquisition).
problem: Vet bills are lumpy and emotional: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay. Only about 5% of US dogs and cats are insured, while premiums rose 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, which invites churn. High-APR deferred-interest cards are the fallback. Meanwhile VPP payouts are small, abstract and easily ignored, even though dispatch is real (580 MW from 140,000 California batteries on September 9, 2026).
solution: Owners assign payouts to a Pet Reserve that auto-pays insurance premiums and pre-funds vet bills at partner clinics. Once the balance builds, they can draw an advance repaid from future dispatch payments, underwritten on battery telemetry and contracted programs. Start with credits and premium payments only, and add advances through a bank or lender partner once the data is proven.
why_now: VPPs are now large enough to have contracted, metered payout streams (Base Power raised $1B with a 500+ MWh fleet; Sunrun/Tesla dispatch). Pet insurance repricing is pushing owners to look for offsets, and no aggregator owns a consumer-finance layer.
revenue_model: Referral bounty from pet insurers ($50-150 per policy), retention/SaaS fee from aggregators or retailers, and interest or fee spread on repayable advances via a lending partner.
non_obvious_insight: A battery in a VPP is a telemetry-verified income stream, and it is collateralizable. Converting abstract kWh payouts into 'vet visits' also changes how much owners value flexibility, and the pet emergency is the highest-emotion, lowest-friction use of the credit.
first_30_days: Recruit one small VPP operator or retail energy provider (not Tesla) and 300-500 pet-owning households through battery-owner communities. Launch payout-to-Pet-Fund with premium auto-pay and a referral deal with one insurer. Measure opt-in, retention and how many households use the balance for vet bills. Hold advances until a lending partner and legal review are in place.

title: Pet Continuity Guarantee Funded by Shelters and Hospitals
one_liner: A membership that guarantees an older adult's pet is picked up within hours of a hospitalization and rehomed after death, paid for by the shelters and hospitals that currently absorb the cost.
customer: The payers are county animal-services agencies and shelters, hospital systems and Medicare Advantage plans, and Area Agencies on Aging. Seniors and their adult children pay a small membership.
problem: Seniors delay 911 calls, refuse admission and cut rehab short because 'nobody will feed Biscuit.' Social workers know it and nobody is paid to fix it. When the owner dies or is hospitalized long-term, the animal ends up as an owner surrender at an already crowded shelter. Nonprofit pet-guardianship programs (for example Friends of Strays) and some Meals on Wheels chapters offer emergency foster, but each is a local patchwork with no dispatch, no standard, and no way for a hospital to call at 2 a.m.
solution: Enrollment with a pet profile (vet records, medications, key-holder, behavior notes), a wallet card and a door sticker. A 24/7 dispatch line that ED nurses, discharge planners and EMS can call. A network of background-checked sitters and foster families paid per diem. A contract with a partner shelter for permanent placement, backed by a small pooled fund that acts as a pet trust in a box (roughly $1,500 per animal endowed from memberships and partner contributions). The system tracks response time and avoided surrenders, so a payer can see the return.
why_now: Shelters are running at or over capacity and paying more for intake. Hospitals are under pressure to cut ED boarding, length of stay and against-medical-advice discharges. A pet guardianship program was in the news in September 2025 (Forbes), signaling that shelters now see guardianship as core. About 4 million Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, and over half of adults 50+ own a pet (AARP).
revenue_model: B2G contract of $300-$800 per avoided surrender or per emergency placement. Hospital and health-plan fee of about $3-$6 per enrolled pet-owning member per month. Senior or family membership of $15-$25/month. Dispatch and sitter-coordination fees.
non_obvious_insight: She will never buy 'pet insurance.' She thinks of it as 'who takes Biscuit.' The barrier to care is emotional and logistical, and hospitals and shelters both pay for the consequences without seeing the link. Existing guardianship programs are capped not by adopters but by the lack of a 4-hour dispatch and response system.
first_30_days: Sign one county shelter and one hospital ED or social-work team as pilot partners. Enroll 50 seniors through Meals on Wheels routes and senior centers. Recruit 15 sitters from local sitter platforms with background checks. Track hours to placement and avoided surrenders, and use the numbers to close the first paid contract.

title: Verified Gig Work History via Data-Access Rights
one_liner: Use statutory data-access requests as an API to pull couriers' and drivers' records from platforms, and issue a verified work-history credential they can carry to landlords, lenders and rival platforms.
customer: Couriers, ride-hail drivers, hosts and cleaners in the EU and UK are the users. Payers are letting agents and landlords, credit unions, neobanks and car-leasing firms verifying variable income, and platforms new to a city that want to import proven riders.
problem: Gig income and ratings are locked in platform apps. Screenshots are unverifiable, so lenders and landlords reject workers or demand guarantors. Changing platforms resets reputation to zero, and deactivations are opaque.
solution: An Export Desk. The worker signs a mandate. The service files GDPR access and portability requests to each platform (and requests under the Platform Work Directive as national laws land), normalizes the data into a standard schema, cross-checks it against bank statements, and issues a signed Work History Credential. It carries tenure, 12-month net income with variance, rating percentile, hours and deactivation events, and it can be shared by link or QR with selective disclosure. Pooled volume gives workers a bargaining bloc.
why_now: The EU Platform Work Directive must be transposed by 2 December 2026, and the Commission says no delay is possible. It strengthens workers' rights to information about algorithmic management. Italy has a draft law, Germany and Spain are moving, and the data-access rights already exist under GDPR and UK GDPR.
revenue_model: Free for workers. Lenders and letting agents pay $6-15 per verified pack, new-entrant platforms pay $20-40 per imported worker, and workers can pay about $4 a month for auto-refresh.
non_obvious_insight: When platforms will not offer an API, the statute is the API. Response clocks are slow but predictable. Once thousands of workers use it, platforms will want to build real APIs to avoid processing requests, and you become the neutral verifier they must integrate with.
first_30_days: Partner with a couriers' or drivers' union or a worker-data nonprofit. Onboard 100 couriers in London or Amsterdam. Produce 50 verified packs by filing requests and reconciling with bank data. Sign two letting agents or a credit union to accept the packs as an alternative to guarantors for a pilot.

title: Vacancy-Permit Kit for Half-Empty Offices
one_liner: A sensor and inspection package that keeps half-empty office buildings insurable and safe during the 12-36 months of limbo before resolution.
customer: Special servicers, receivers and owners of office buildings under roughly 31% occupancy or with dark floors, plus lender-placed insurance managers.
problem: Many standard commercial property forms treat a building as vacant unless about 31% of its area is leased and in use, and after 60 days of vacancy exclude vandalism, water damage, theft and glass while cutting other payouts (buildings under renovation are exempt). Meanwhile stagnant plumbing raises Legionella risk, HVAC is wasted, and squatters and fire watch add cost. About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, and resolutions take years.
solution: Flow and temperature sensors with automated flush valves, HVAC setback tied to the building system, AI door and intrusion cameras and documented monthly inspections. Packaged as evidence for a vacancy permit or protective-safeguards endorsement and as reporting to servicers, installed only on dark floors.
why_now: Distress is at record levels with long resolutions, property insurance is costly and restrictive, and IoT and video analytics are cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.30 per sf per year subscription plus $1-3 per sf install, with referral fees from commercial insurance brokers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is writing about conversion, but nobody services the limbo period where value leaks through insurance denials and stagnant water. A few dollars of sensors can be cheaper than one uninsured water loss.
first_30_days: Partner with two commercial brokers who place vacant-building coverage. Pilot at two receiver-owned buildings for about $5K each. Ask an insurer to accept the protocol in writing.

title: Disposition Authority Registry for Chosen Family
one_liner: A verified registry that lets hospitals and funeral homes instantly find out who legally controls a person's body when that person is not the state's default next of kin.
customer: Solo agers, unmarried long-term partners, LGBTQ+ elders, people estranged from family, and blended-family couples pay $59 to register. Estate-planning attorneys, senior and LGBTQ+ service organizations, and hospice or palliative social work teams are the channel and secondary payers.
problem: State statutes rank who controls disposition: spouse, adult children, parents, siblings. An unmarried partner of 30 years can be shut out by a child who hasn't spoken to the deceased in a decade. When it goes wrong, the body sits in refrigeration for days or weeks while lawyers argue, and the funeral home is stuck because releasing to the wrong person means being sued. Many states allow a written designation of an agent, but witness and notary rules differ, and the signed document is in a drawer or a safe deposit box that no one can open at 2 a.m.
solution: Attorney-reviewed, state-specific designation forms completed through a remote-notary and e-sign flow. The signed document goes into a timestamped registry, with a wallet card and a phone lock-screen QR. A 24/7 verification line and API lets hospital social workers, medical examiner offices and funeral homes ask 'is there a designated agent for this person?' The designated agent is auto-notified. The record also stores preferences (cremation or burial, preferred funeral home, link to any pre-need contract).
why_now: The US has a fast-growing population of solo agers and 'elder orphans': never-married, childless, divorced or estranged. The cohort of same-sex couples who married after 2015 is now entering the age of dying. Remote online notarization and electronic signature of estate documents are now widely accepted. Healthcare advance-directive registries exist, but almost none cover disposition.
revenue_model: $59 one-time registration plus $12/year for renewal and verification upkeep. Attorney and organization white-label at $25 per registrant. Hospice, hospital and health-system site licenses at $2,000-$5,000/year for verification access. Verification is free to funeral homes so adoption is frictionless.
non_obvious_insight: The ugliest funeral disputes are almost never about money, they're about who has the pen. Funeral homes carry all the legal risk of releasing to the wrong person, so they will champion and actively check any credible registry. Everyone built registries for the living person's medical wishes, but nobody built one for the body. That is the gap where an insider watches families fight in the arrangement office.
first_30_days: Launch in three states whose statutes expressly recognize a written designation of agent. Partner with a local LGBTQ+ senior center, an elder-orphan or solo-ager meetup, and two estate attorneys who will co-host workshops. Get ten funeral homes to sign a one-page pledge to check the registry on every first call. Sell registrations at senior-center and library workshops and via a 'chosen family' landing page. Target 150-200 registrations and use the first funeral-home lookup as the case study.

title: AI-Washing Forensics for Investors and Buyers
one_liner: A five-day outside-in diligence product that tests whether an AI startup's product is real autonomy, its revenue is real, and its users are human.
customer: Seed-to-growth investors (micro-VCs, corporate VCs, growth funds), corporate M&A teams, venture lenders, and enterprise procurement teams buying AI vendors.
problem: Builder.ai's 2025 insolvency (marketed AI, with heavy human labour behind it), the 2025 DOJ case against the founder of Nate, and a wave of 'ARR' made of pilots, credits and bot traffic show that diligence rests on demos, reference calls and a quality-of-earnings that never tests the technology claim.
solution: A black-box harness and data-room protocol. It covers interaction testing at scale (latency and variance signatures that reveal human-in-the-loop or third-party model calls), unit-economics reconstruction (tokens versus price versus gross margin), revenue reality (read-only Stripe and bank data plus contract sampling to separate pilot, committed, credit-funded and refunded revenue), audience authenticity (bot and agent share of users from server logs), and independent reference call-backs. Output is a 'Reality Report' with confidence intervals.
why_now: Builder.ai (2025) and Delve (2026) reset investor trust. AI-startup ARR claims are exploding, and more than half of web traffic is now automated, which inflates 'users'. Investors are compressing diligence to days, and AI products are uniquely testable from outside because you can hit the endpoint.
revenue_model: $15-40k per full report paid by the investor (often reimbursed at close), a $5k lite scan, and annual portfolio-monitoring retainers for funds.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume diligence must rely on the founder's data. AI products can be tested from the outside, so the scarce thing is independence and speed, and the buyer of speed is an investor with a 48-hour exclusivity window.
first_30_days: Offer five free 'reality scans' to angel syndicates and micro-VC partners on live deals in exchange for named case studies. Build the harness with two ML engineers and one forensic accountant. Set pricing after three wins.

title: Reef Mixtapes for Oyster Hatcheries and Reefs
one_liner: Underwater speakers and a licensed library of healthy-reef soundscapes that lure oyster larvae to settle in hatchery tanks and restoration sites.
customer: Oyster hatcheries and remote-setting operations, oyster farmers, and restoration NGOs and state shellfish agencies such as those running large reef programs.
problem: Larval settlement is a costly bottleneck: eyed larvae are expensive to raise and many fail to set on cultch. Restoration reefs built on bare bottom get poor recruitment because they are silent, while healthy reefs act like acoustic beacons.
solution: A plug-in kit of a waterproof speaker, a controller and a subscription to species- and region-specific reef sound libraries recorded on healthy local reefs (snapping-shrimp crackle in the 1.5-20 kHz range). It ships with a built-in split-tank A/B protocol so any hatchery can measure the settlement gain in a week. Restoration clients can pay per acre on measured recruitment. Later products: playback buoys and acoustic tuning per species.
why_now: The science is now credible and publicised. Lab playbacks showed more oyster settlement under reef sound than under soft-bottom sound or silence (Lillis et al., PLOS ONE 2013), and later work reported large increases. In July 2026 WHOI, with The Nature Conservancy Massachusetts and shellfish constables, began a two-year effort to build a 'New England mixtape' for farmers and restorers. Rugged hydrophones and speakers are cheap. Nobody has yet packaged this for commerce.
revenue_model: Hardware kit at roughly $600-1,500, a library subscription of $50-150 per month per site, and performance-based restoration contracts (for example a share of measured settlement gains or per-acre fees). Longer term, license the sound and response dataset to acoustic-restoration players.
non_obvious_insight: Larvae navigate by ear, and degraded reefs are literally silent, so sound is a cheap cue you can sell. The defensible asset is the proprietary library of local recordings plus the settlement-response data by species and region. Commercial-hatchery effect sizes are still unproven, so the honest first product is the A/B testing rig and pay-on-results pricing, which turns scientific uncertainty into the sales pitch.
first_30_days: Buy two hydrophones and two speakers. Get three small hatcheries to run split-tank A/B settlement counts with a simple protocol, and record one healthy reef per region. Publish the first results and convert the hatcheries with the strongest lift into paying $1,500 kits.

title: Notary for AI Agents' Authority to Sign
one_liner: A registry of signed, scoped, revocable 'mandates' that let a company's AI agents prove to counterparties what they may commit to, with a legal opinion and an insurer behind each.
customer: SMBs and mid-market firms deploying purchasing, AR/AP, sales-ops and scheduling agents (finance and ops leads), the fintech and AP-automation platforms embedding those agents, and the vendors on the receiving end.
problem: Agents now email vendors, accept quotes, change orders and click 'I agree'. Counterparties cannot tell whether an agent had authority, whose it is, or its spend limit, and companies cannot prove afterward what they authorized. Contract-formation doctrine (electronic-agent provisions, apparent authority) predates this. Payment protocols carry payment mandates, not authority to bind.
solution: Phase one: a legal template and JSON mandate schema (principal, agent identity, scope by category and counterparty, dollar cap, expiry, escalation), signed as verifiable credentials, with a public verify API and a revocation registry, an audit log, and a law-firm opinion letter on enforceability for the first US states. Any counterparty agent can call a check_mandate MCP tool. Phase two: an MGA-backed insurance product for agent commitments up to the mandate cap.
why_now: MCP and agent-payment protocols emerged in 2025 and small-firm agent adoption is visible now (60+ firms on MyCase's connector in one month), yet the contract-authority layer between payments and law has no owner (background, verify).
revenue_model: $50-500/month per business, per-verification fees for high-volume counterparties, an insurance premium share, and $10-25k enterprise opinion-letter packages.
non_obvious_insight: Payment rails answer 'can this agent pay?' while the law asks 'was it authorized to bind?', and that depends on documented delegation, the same problem powers of attorney and corporate resolutions solved for humans. Whoever sets the schema counterparties check becomes the standard.
first_30_days: Draft the mandate schema and template with a partner law firm and publish an open spec. Pilot with five procurement or AP-agent startups, ship the verify API, get three design partners to put an authority header in agent emails, and open talks with two MGAs.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that mines a buyer's 2025-26 supplier invoices for 'tariff surcharge' lines and recovers a share of the IEEPA refunds those suppliers are now collecting.
customer: Multi-unit restaurant and retail franchisees, contractor purchasing co-ops, and mid-market distributors' customers that paid itemized tariff, freight or 'inflation' surcharges to suppliers who were the importer of record. They pay a 20-30% success fee on money recovered.
problem: IEEPA duty refunds go only to the importer of record (IOR) or a party the IOR designates. Buyers who paid the tariff as a surcharge or a higher price get nothing unless they ask. AutoZone booked about $96M and Cracker Barrel $15M, with MillerKnoll $16.5M and Worthington $4M. Downstream buyers have no visibility into what their suppliers recovered and no process to ask for it.
solution: Read-only inbox and AP connectors pull 2025-26 invoices and extract surcharge, 'tariff', 'duty' and 'trade cost recovery' line items. The system estimates each supplier's IEEPA exposure from public import-manifest data. It checks the supplier's terms for pass-back language, such as 'surcharge will be removed or refunded if tariffs are rescinded'. It then generates a claim letter with an offer to accept credit memos or to have the supplier name the buyer as the CBP Form 4811 notify party so the refund routes to the buyer. A second module audits new diesel and fuel surcharges against the contract formula and the EIA diesel index. Claims are sent to the top 20 suppliers per buyer, and unclaimed money is tracked to closure.
why_now: CBP's CAPE portal opened in 2026 and is issuing refunds within 60-90 days of an accepted declaration. Refunds are landing in Q3-Q4 2026 P&Ls as one-time gains. Suppliers are least defensible in the first months after booking a windfall and will negotiate to keep customer goodwill. Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 year over year, so a wave of fresh surcharge invoices is arriving that nobody audits.
revenue_model: A 20-30% contingency fee on recovered refunds and credits, plus $199-$999/month for continuous surcharge auditing (fuel, energy, 'regulatory recovery' fees) once the first recovery lands.
non_obvious_insight: The refund windfall is a transfer from customers to importers, and the CFOs say so. AutoZone's CFO said 'the refund environment was deflationary, and the industry likely would have raised prices faster if both retailers and suppliers hadn't received cost relief' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Cracker Barrel booked a $15M refund and MillerKnoll $16.5M, worth 180 bps of gross margin (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/ and https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). CBP states 'Only the IOR ... or the authorized customs broker ... may file' and never mentions downstream buyers, couriers or DDP shipments (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds). Every downstream claim is therefore a negotiation, and the buyer who holds the 2025 invoices has the leverage. Nobody is selling that to the buyer side. The legal caveat is that the buyer needs an explicit surcharge line or contract language to have a real claim, so the product should target only those cases.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-8 restaurant franchisee groups or contractor purchasing co-ops through franchisee associations and buying-group managers, with a free 'we only get paid if you get paid' offer. Export 2025 AP data or forward invoice PDFs, then have an analyst plus an LLM extraction script build a surcharge ledger for the top 15 suppliers each. Send the first 30 claim letters with a one-page template that cites the refund program and asks for credit or 4811 routing. Have a supply-chain lawyer review the template. Aim to close the first paid recovery within 60-75 days.
